entry: Video that becomes widely popular through rapid Internet sharing, usually on video-sharing sites such as [[YouTube]], on [[Social media|social media]] and by [[Email|email]]. Viral videos may be serious or emotional, but many rely on entertainment and [[Comedy|comedy]]. Early examples include the television sketches "Lazy Sunday" and "Dick in a Box", Numa Numa videos and "Chocolate Rain." [[Gangnam Style]] (2012) received one billion views in five months and was the most-viewed YouTube video from 2012 until "Despacito" (2017).

Indian cricketer and former all-format captain of the national team. A right-handed batter, he has the most One Day International centuries and the second-most international centuries, with 86 across all formats. He is the leading run-scorer in the [[Indian Premier League]]. Kohli captained the 2008 U19 World Cup-winning team and was a key member of the Indian teams that won the [[Cricket World Cup|2011 Cricket World Cup]] and the 2024 T20 World Cup. He has won ten ICC Awards, the most of any player. He announced his retirement from T20I cricket after the 2024 T20 World Cup and from Test cricket on May 12, 2025.

Mass shooting at Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University in Blacksburg, [[Virginia]]. Seung-Hui Cho, a 23-year-old undergraduate, fatally shot two people in a dormitory and then 30 more at Norris Hall, a classroom building, before killing himself. The attacks killed 32 people and wounded 17 others, the deadliest U.S. mass shooting until the Pulse nightclub shooting. The shooting prompted debate about gun laws and gaps in [[Mental health|mental health]] care. Cho had been declared mentally ill in 2005 and was not institutionalized, so he could buy guns.

English modernist writer who pioneered the use of stream-of-consciousness narration. Born into an affluent intellectual family in [[London]], she became a founding member of the Bloomsbury Group. She began publishing professionally in 1904 and rose to prominence in the interwar period with novels including *Mrs Dalloway* (1925), *To the Lighthouse* (1927) and *Orlando* (1928). Her feminist essay *A Room of One's Own* (1929) was followed by *Three Guineas* (1938), which explores the roots of [[Fascism|fascism]] in society. With her husband, Leonard Woolf, she founded the Hogarth Press in 1917, which published much of her work. Her work became central to 1970s feminist criticism and has been translated into more than 50 languages.

U.S. state, with its capital at Richmond and a population of 8.8 million. Virginia was the site of the first permanent English colony in the [[New World]], founded at Jamestown in 1607 by the London Company. Virginians fought in the [[American Revolution]]. During the [[American Civil War|Civil War]] the state joined the Confederacy, and northwestern counties loyal to the Union separated as West Virginia in 1863. The General Assembly, established in July 1619, is the oldest extant law-making body in North America. Virginia Beach is its most populous city.

North American marsupial of the opossum family, found from southern [[Canada]] to northern [[Costa Rica]]. It is the northernmost marsupial in the world. A solitary, nocturnal animal about the size of a domestic [[Cat|cat]], it is an opportunistic omnivore. Its ancestors evolved in South America, and the genus entered North America about 0.8 million years ago. Since 1900 it has expanded its range northward, including into most of New England and southern Ontario.

State of never having engaged in [[Sexual intercourse|sexual intercourse]]. Virginity is a social construct with no operational definition, so its meaning varies. Heterosexual people may or may not consider virginity lost only through penile-vaginal penetration, while people of other sexual orientations often include oral, anal or manual sex. Religious rituals for regaining virginity exist in many cultures. Some people who practice [[Celibacy|celibacy]] after losing their virginity consider themselves born-again virgins. Traditions have placed special value on virginity, predominantly for unmarried women, associated with purity and honor. It has no legal consequences in most modern societies. Feminist scholars argue that no standardized medical definition of virginity exists and no scientifically verifiable proof of virginity loss exists. The first known English use of the word appears in a Middle English manuscript of about 1200.

Galaxy cluster in the constellation Virgo, centered 53.8 ± 0.3 Mly (16.5 ± 0.1 Mpc) away. It contains approximately 1,300 member galaxies, possibly up to 2,000, and forms the heart of the [[Virgo Supercluster]], which contains the [[Local Group]]. Its mass is estimated at 1.2×10¹⁵ M☉ within about 2.2 Mpc. The giant elliptical galaxy [[Messier 87]] contains a [[Supermassive black hole|supermassive black hole]] whose [[Event horizon|event horizon]] was observed by the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration in 2019. The cluster's brightest member is the elliptical galaxy Messier 49. Three subclusters are merging to form a single cluster, which suggests that the Virgo Cluster is dynamically young and still forming.

Supercluster of galaxies containing the [[Virgo Cluster]] and the [[Local Group]]. At least 100 galaxy groups and clusters lie within its diameter of 45 megaparsecs (147 million light-years). It is one of about 10 million superclusters in the [[Observable universe|observable universe]]. Its main body, the Virgo Strand, connects the Hydra-Centaurus and Perseus-Pisces superclusters, and it is part of the Pisces–Cetus Supercluster Complex, a very large galaxy filament. A 2014 study indicated that the Virgo Supercluster is part of the larger [[Laniakea Supercluster]], centered on the [[Great Attractor]]. The Local Group lies near one edge of the Virgo Supercluster, and the supercluster's volume is roughly 7,000 times that of the Local Group.

Trait of excellence, which may be moral, social or intellectual. In human ethics, a virtue is a disposition to choose actions that show high moral standards, even when this may be unnecessary from a utilitarian perspective. The opposite of virtue is vice. The Latin word *virtus* was used by the ancient Romans for all excellent qualities of men. In [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]], the goddess Ma'at personified truth, balance, order, law and justice. [[Plato]] listed four cardinal virtues: prudence (wisdom), fortitude, temperance and justice, and added piety. [[Aristotle]] defined a virtue as a point between a deficiency and an excess of a trait, chosen under the guidance of reason.

City in the Indian state of [[Andhra Pradesh]], between the Eastern Ghats and the coast of the [[Bay of Bengal]]. It is the largest and most populous city in Andhra Pradesh and the second-largest on India's east coast after [[Chennai]]. Known as the shipbuilding capital of India, it has the oldest shipyard in India and the only natural harbor on the east coast. Visakhapatnam Port is the fifth-busiest cargo port in India. The city hosts the headquarters of the Indian Navy's Eastern Naval Command. Historically a trading port with the [[Middle East]] and Rome, it came under [[East India Company]] control in 1804 and remained under British rule until Indian independence in 1947.

Archipelago in the central [[Philippines]], one of the country's three principal geographical divisions, along with [[Luzon]] and [[Mindanao]]. Its major islands are Panay, Negros, Cebu, Bohol, Leyte and Samar, primarily surrounding the Visayan Sea. The Visayas are divided into four administrative regions: Western Visayas (pop. 4.86 million), Negros Island Region (pop. 4.90 million), Central Visayas (6.64 million) and Eastern Visayas (4.63 million). The exact origin of the name is unknown. The first documented use may be by the Song-era Chinese official Zhao Rugua, who recorded raiders of the [[Fujian]] coast in the late 12th century. Spanish colonists called Visayans *Pintados* ("the painted ones") for their full-body tattooing.

Property of a fluid that quantifies the resistance force acting when fluid parcels move relative to one another. In liquids, viscosity arises from cohesive molecular forces, and in gases from molecular collisions. For liquids it corresponds to the informal concept of thickness; syrup has a higher viscosity than [[Water|water]]. Viscosity is defined as force multiplied by time divided by area, and its SI units are pascal-seconds. Except in [[Superfluidity|superfluids]], no fluid has zero viscosity, because the [[Second law of thermodynamics|second law of thermodynamics]] requires positive viscosity. Viscosity of a Newtonian fluid does not vary significantly with the rate of deformation. The word derives from the [[Latin]] *viscum* ("mistletoe").

Major deity of [[Hinduism|Hinduism]], known as the Preserver within the Trimurti. In [[Vaishnavism|Vaishnavism]], Vishnu is the Supreme Being who creates, protects and transforms the universe. Also known as Narayana and Hari, he is depicted sleeping on the serpent Shesha in the primeval ocean with his consort, [[Lakshmi]]. Whenever the world is threatened with evil, Vishnu descends in the form of an [[Avatar|avatar]] to restore cosmic order and protect [[Dharma|dharma]]. The ten primary avatars are the Dashavatara, of which [[Rama]] and [[Krishna]] are the most worshipped, with temples across India and beyond. Vishnu rose to prominence in post-Vedic times, and his name means "all pervasive."

Band of the [[Electromagnetic spectrum|electromagnetic spectrum]] visible to the human eye. A typical human eye responds to wavelengths from about 380 to 750 nanometers, roughly 400–790 terahertz, though the boundaries vary by individual. Pink and magenta are absent from the spectrum because they require a mixture of wavelengths. In the 17th century, [[Isaac Newton|Isaac Newton]] showed with prisms that white light is composed of colors and first used the word spectrum in print in 1671. Newton originally divided the spectrum into six named colors and later added indigo as a seventh. Because clean air scatters [[Blue|blue]] light more than red, the midday sky appears blue.

Germanic kingdom that occupied southwestern France and most of the Iberian Peninsula from the 5th to the 8th century. It was created when the [[Visigoths]] were settled as foederati in Aquitaine in 418. The kingdom lost most of its Gallic territory to the [[Franks]] in the early 6th century, but it expanded in Iberia. The Visigoths renounced [[Arianism|Arianism]] in 589. The Visigothic Code, completed in 654, abolished separate laws for Hispano-Romans and Visigoths. Byzantine forces held southern Hispania until 624. Umayyad troops conquered most of the kingdom from 711 to 719, though the northern reaches remained in Christian hands, where the kingdom of [[Asturias]] emerged.

Gothic people of late antiquity and the early Middle Ages. Probably descended from the Thervingi, they were first united under [[Alaric I]], whose forces sacked Rome in 410. In 418 they were settled as foederati in southern Gaul, establishing a kingdom at [[Toulouse]]. Defeat by the [[Franks]] at Vouillé in 507 ended their rule in Gaul, but the kingdom consolidated in Spain and Portugal. Under King Reccared I they converted from Arian Christianity to Nicene Christianity in 589. Their Visigothic Code (654) abolished legal distinctions between Goths and Romans. The kingdom collapsed in 711, and the [[Reconquista]] began in the north.

Longest river in [[Poland]] and the longest river draining into the Baltic Sea, at 1,047 kilometres (651 miles). Its drainage basin covers 193,960 sq km, of which 168,868 sq km is in Poland. The Vistula rises at Barania Góra in the Silesian Beskids of the Carpathian Mountains, at 1,220 meters above sea level. It flows through Kraków, Sandomierz, [[Warsaw]], Toruń and Gdańsk, and enters the Baltic through a delta of six main branches. The river is Poland's most important waterway and a national symbol, and the phrase "Land on the Vistula" can mean Poland. Its name gave the Weichselian glaciation, the last glacial period in northern Europe.

headword: Visual arts of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas
sort_key: visual arts of the indigenous peoples of the americas
entry: Visual artistic practices of the Indigenous peoples of North, Central and South America from ancient times to the present. Portable arts include painting, [[Textile|basketry and textiles]], and [[Photography|photography]], while monumental works include architecture, land art and [[Mural|murals]]. The oldest known art in the Americas is a carved bone, possibly from a [[Mammoth|mammoth]] or [[Mastodon|mastodon]], dating to about 11,000 BCE and found near Vero Beach, Florida. The Cooper Bison Skull, from about 8,050 BCE, is the oldest painted object in North America. Modern Inuit art began in the late 1940s, and Western museums have classified precontact work as pre-Columbian art. Scholars increasingly seek to interpret the works from Indigenous perspectives.

Partial or total inability of [[Visual perception|visual perception]]. Without treatment such as corrective eyewear, it may cause difficulty with daily tasks, including reading and walking. The most common causes worldwide are uncorrected [[Refractive error|refractive errors]] (43%), cataracts (33%) and [[Glaucoma|glaucoma]] (2%). Cataracts are the most common cause of blindness. Visual impairment can also result from brain problems due to [[Stroke|stroke]], premature birth or trauma. The [[World Health Organization]] estimates that 80% of visual impairment is preventable or curable. As of 2015, 940 million people had some degree of vision loss, including 246 million with low vision and 39 million who were blind. Most people with poor vision live in the developing world and are over the age of 50.

Ability to detect light and use it to form an image of the surrounding environment. Photodetection without image formation is classified as light sensing. Most vertebrates have photopic (daytime) vision, scotopic (night) vision, or both. Visual perception detects light in the [[Visible spectrum|visible spectrum]] reflected by objects or emitted by light sources. It is an active process in which the brain interprets and organizes sensory information, influenced by prior knowledge, expectations and context. Visual perception is also adaptive and shaped by lifelong experience and changing cognitive capacities. The physiological components involved are called the [[Visual system|visual system]], which is studied in [[Neuroscience|neuroscience]], psychology and molecular biology under the name vision science.

Physiological basis of [[Perception|visual perception]], associated with the [[Eye|eye]]. It is divided into the optical system, including the cornea and lens, and the neural system, including the retina and visual cortex. It detects and interprets light to construct an image and a mental model of the surrounding environment. Its tasks include stereopsis, depth perception, motion perception, pattern recognition and [[Color vision|color vision]], which together support object identification. Non-image-forming functions include the pupillary light reflex and circadian photoentrainment. The neuropsychological side of visual information processing is known as [[Visual perception|visual perception]], an abnormality of which is called [[Visual impairment|visual impairment]], and a complete absence of which is called blindness. This entry describes the human visual system, which is representative of [[Mammal|mammalian]] vision.

Essential B vitamin, also called cobalamin. It is needed for metabolism in every cell, particularly DNA synthesis, myelin synthesis and the maturation of red blood cells. It is synthesized exclusively by certain [[Archaea|archaea]] and [[Bacteria|bacteria]]. Natural sources include [[Meat|meat]], shellfish, [[Liver|liver]], [[Fish|fish]], poultry, eggs and dairy products. Deficiency is uncommon in healthy adults, but it is a significant concern in the elderly, who may have impaired absorption, and it is related to [[Dementia|dementia]]. Deficiency can cause [[Anemia|anemia]] and neuropathy, and in pregnancy it increases the risk of miscarriage and neural tube defects.

Water-soluble vitamin, also called ascorbate, found in [[Citrus|citrus]] fruits and other foods. It is essential for tissue repair and collagen formation, and it is important for [[Immune system|immune system]] function. Most animals synthesize their own vitamin C, but higher primates, including humans, must obtain it from their diet. Vitamin C is used to prevent and treat scurvy. Large doses may cause gastrointestinal discomfort and headache. It was discovered in 1912, isolated in 1928, and in 1933 became the first vitamin to be chemically produced. Partly for this discovery, Albert Szent-Györgyi received the 1937 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Group of fat-soluble compounds that increase intestinal absorption of calcium. The most important forms are vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) and vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol). Unlike other vitamins, it is only conditionally essential, because the skin synthesizes it from ultraviolet B radiation in [[Sunlight|sunlight]]. It is also obtained from fortified [[Milk|milk]], breakfast cereals and [[Dietary supplement|supplements]]. The vitamin was discovered in 1922 during an effort to identify the dietary deficiency that caused rickets in children. Its biologically active form, calcitriol, attaches to vitamin D receptors throughout the body.
